title: Siberian Traps
description: Large region of volcanic rock in Russia
wiki_lead: The Siberian Traps (Russian: Сибирские траппы, romanized: Sibirskiye trappy) are a large region of volcanic rock, known as a large igneous province, in Siberia, Russia. Large volumes of basaltic lava covered a large expanse of Siberia in a flood basalt event. The massive eruptive event that formed the traps is one of the largest-known volcanic events in the last 500 million years. The eruptions continued for roughly two million years and spanned the Permian–Triassic boundary, or P–T boundary, which occurred around 251.9 million years ago. The Siberian Traps are believed to be the primary cause of the Permian–Triassic extinction event, the most severe extinction event in the geologic record. Subsequent periods of Siberian Traps activity have been linked to smaller biotic crises, including the Smithian–Spathian, Olenekian–Anisian, Middle-Late Anisian and Anisian–Ladinian extinction events. Today, the area is covered by about 7 million km2 (3 million sq mi) of basaltic rock, with a volume of around 4 million km3 (1 million cu mi).
wiki_excerpt:
The Siberian Traps (Russian: Сибирские траппы, romanized: Sibirskiye trappy) are a large region of volcanic rock, known as a large igneous province, in Siberia, Russia. Large volumes of basaltic lava covered a large expanse of Siberia in a flood basalt event. The massive eruptive event that formed the traps is one of the largest-known volcanic events in the last 500 million years. The eruptions continued for roughly two million years and spanned the Permian–Triassic boundary, or P–T boundary, which occurred around 251.9 million years ago. The Siberian Traps are believed to be the primary cause of the Permian–Triassic extinction event, the most severe extinction event in the geologic record. Subsequent periods of Siberian Traps activity have been linked to smaller biotic crises, including the Smithian–Spathian, Olenekian–Anisian, Middle-Late Anisian and Anisian–Ladinian extinction events. Today, the area is covered by about 7 million km2 (3 million sq mi) of basaltic rock, with a volume of around 4 million km3 (1 million cu mi).


Etymology
The term "trap" has been used in geology since 1785–1795 for such rock formations. It is derived from the Swedish word for stairs ("trappa") and refers to the step-like hills forming the landscape of the region.


Formation

The source of the Siberian Traps basaltic rock has been attributed to a mantle plume which rose until it reached the bottom of the Earth's crust, producing volcanic eruptions through the Siberian Craton. It has been suggested that, as the Earth's lithospheric plates moved over the mantle plume (the Iceland plume), the plume had earlier produced the Viluy traps to the east, then the Siberian Traps in the Permian and Triassic periods, and produced volcanic activity on the floor of the Arctic Ocean in the Jurassic and Cretaceous, and then generating volcanic activity in Iceland. Other plate tectonic causes have also been suggested. Another possible cause may be the impact that formed the Wilkes Land crater in Antarctica, which is estimated to have occurred around the same time and been nearly antipodal to the traps.
The main source of rock in this formation is basalt, but both mafic and felsic rocks are present, so this formation is officially called a Flood Basalt Province. The inclusion of mafic and felsic rock indicates multiple other eruptions that occurred and coincided with the one-million-year-long set of eruptions that created the majority of the basaltic layers. The traps are divided into sections based on their chemical, stratigraphical and petrographical composition.
The Siberian Traps are underlain by the Tungus Syneclise, a large sedimentary basin containing thick sequences of Early-Mid-Paleozoic-aged carbonate and evaporite deposits, as well as Carboniferous–Permian-aged coal-bearing clastic rocks. When heated, such as by igneous intrusions, these rocks are capable of emitting large amounts of toxic and greenhouse gases.

grok_lead: The Siberian Traps form one of Earth's largest large igneous provinces, comprising extensive flood basalts, sills, dikes, and other intrusive rocks primarily exposed across northwestern Siberia in Russia, with preserved outcrops spanning from the Taimyr Peninsula to the Kazakhstan border and underlying much of the West Siberian Basin. The province covers an area of approximately 7 million square kilometers and has an estimated total volume of about 4 million cubic kilometers, though these figures account for significant erosion and burial of original materials, with intrusive components comprising up to two-thirds of the total. The main eruptive phase occurred rapidly between approximately 252.3 and 251.4 million years ago, coinciding with the Permian-Triassic boundary and lasting less than 1 million years, though magmatism initiated slightly earlier around 254 million years ago and continued in pulses until about 240 million years ago. This voluminous outpouring of predominantly tholeiitic basalts is linked to a mantle plume origin and is considered the chief trigger for the end-Permian mass extinction, the most devastating in geological history, which eradicated roughly 96% of marine species and 70% of terrestrial vertebrate species through mechanisms including massive greenhouse gas emissions, acid rain, ocean acidification, and widespread anoxia. Geologically, the Siberian Traps consist of layered lava flows up to 3 kilometers thick in places, such as the Norilsk-Talnakh region, interspersed with tuffs, pyroclastics, and sills intruded into underlying sedimentary basins rich in organic carbon and evaporites. High-precision U-Pb dating of zircons from ash beds and intrusions reveals at least two major magmatic pulses: an initial effusive phase around 252 million years ago, followed by an intrusive sill phase around 251.9 million years ago that preheated and volatilized coal-bearing sediments, releasing thermogenic methane and COâ, with subsequent effusive stages that flooded the landscape with lava. The interaction of hot magmas with Siberian platform sediments amplified environmental impacts, as contact aureoles around sills baked vast quantities of carbonates and hydrocarbons, contributing to hyperwarming that raised global temperatures by 8â10Â°C and disrupted the carbon cycle. The extinction's severity is evidenced by fossil records showing abrupt declines in diversity across marine (e.g., ammonoids, brachiopods) and terrestrial (e.g., dicynodonts, insects) biotas, with recovery taking millions of years into the Early Triassic. Their remnants today include dramatic plateaus like the Putorana, a UNESCO World Heritage site showcasing stepped basalt landscapes. Ongoing research uses isotopic analyses (e.g., nickel, mercury) to trace volcanic aerosols and further elucidate the kill mechanisms, underscoring the Traps' role as a paradigm for LIP-driven environmental catastrophes.
